extracted.intended_audience: scholars/practitioners of natural philosophy and optics (learned readers, observers of optical phenomena)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and diagnostic guidance (observational rules, geometric procedures, material criteria) for studying optical phenomena: light, colors, mirrors, rainbows/irides, coronas, twilight, comets, and focused reflection as presented in a medieval natural-philosophical treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three species of light (recta, reflexa, refracta)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds/species of luminous appearance in transparent bodies: recta (direct), reflexa (reflected), and refracta (refracted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct (recta) shows things as they are; refracted (refracta) shows things altered; reflected (reflexa), like mirrors, presents images as from specular reflection. Use this classification when diagnosing why an object appears altered, displaced, or mirrored in a transparent medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and diagnostic of 'clarum' / 'perspicuum' bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: A body that is 'clarum' or 'perspicuum' admits the image of light without requiring pores; it transmits the image (imago lucis) though not light as a body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between bodies that simply transmit light and those that transmit the image; solids can receive rays and heat more readily because rays are received into their substance. When analyzing image formation, determine whether the medium is perspicuous (permits clear image formation) or merely illuminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror/speculum material and shape criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of reflecting material and its shape affects image fidelity: metallic mirrors (steel, silver) yield more exact images than glass (vitrum/crystallum), though metals tarnish more easily while glass is more durable unless broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer metallic specula for accuracy of image; expect glass to be more durable but potentially less exact and more liable to vitiation in humid conditions. Also note concave/convex and uneven surfaces distort images (cavities and convexities give false images). Use shape and material considerations when constructing or evaluating mirrors for experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and mechanism for rainbow/iris formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Iris (rainbow) is produced by reflection/refraction from drops/denser parts of clouds (a hollow/delineated cloud of drops). The colors arise from the way solar rays are reflected/refracted in these drops; multiple concentric circles and color bands result from geometry of reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iris appears when a hollow-like cloud composed of many droplets reflects solar rays perpendicularly in parts; if the cloud is not hollow or lacks enough drops, reflection is altered. Observe droplet-filled clouds against the sun to reproduce iris; compare to reflection in water drops or glass to confirm similar color ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric alignment for observing a rainbow (center-line rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To see an iris, the eye, the sun, and the centre of the iris must lie on one straight line; the visible form will usually be a semicircle when the sun is on the horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure observer alignment: draw the line from eye through the sun to the supposed centre of the rainbow; if the centre lies on the horizon (sun at horizon), a semicircular form appears. Use this geometrical relation when predicting rainbow appearance and extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for measuring rainbow angular radius and size
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the arc/angle of the rainbow by geometric construction: identify the centre (line from sun through eye), construct triangles using chord/arc tables, and use proportions/trigonometry with assumed vapor altitude to compute the rainbow's semi-diameter and distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: find the centre under the horizon, measure relevant angles (via chord/arc tables), form right triangles (using tables of chord and arc), compute proportions (linear ratios), and derive the semi-diameter and apparent size. Account for altitude of vapours (vapours rarely ascend above a maximum), which affects when twilight and rainbow begin/appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color order and structure of the iris
rubrics_metrics.description: The iris consists of concentric color rings whose order depends on the manner of reflection: inner circle bluish (caeruleus), middle green (viridis), outer saffron/croceus, with transitional gradations (e.g., green between blue and saffron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color arises from the gradation of illumination across the reflecting droplets and from which portion of the reflecting circle contributes; inner rings correspond to rays reflected at different parts of the droplet ensemble. Expect transitions rather than abrupt bands; use this to interpret observed rainbow color sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between iris, parelia (parhelia), and corona
rubrics_metrics.description: Iris (rainbow) results from reflection/refraction in droplets at distance; parelia/parelix (mock suns) are side images of the sun produced by reflection in peripheral droplets (appear as extra suns); corona is a circular colored ring produced by reflection about a dense central cloud and indicates a dense cloud layer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose phenomena by shape and source: parelia are lateral bright images often near the sun; corona is a circular colored ring centered on a cloud patch (not imagined by the eye); corona often signals dense cloud and forthcoming winds if parts persist or dissipate. Use presence/shape to forecast weather changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather-sign criteria from coronas and irides
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistent corona or irides indicate a dense cloud layer that may herald winds, storms, or changes; the part of the corona that remains or dissipates gives an indication of wind direction and whether the cloud will spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts of the corona persist while others dissipate, expect wind from the direction corresponding to the persisting part. A long-lasting corona / dense cloud suggests incoming winds and changes; a thin/transient iris suggests lighter, transient vapors. Use these optical signs as meteorological indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for judging whether comets are aerial (in the air) or celestial
rubrics_metrics.description: Comets often originate in vapours (aerial region) because tails point away from the sun, their motion patterns (triplex motion: with sunward/anti-sunward components and latitude motion), and because longstanding burning for months within the element is implausible; yet multiple tests are proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate: tail orientation (always opposite sun), duration (months of burning unlikely in a single element), observed motion relative to planets (speed differences compared to lunar motion), and whether neighboring vapours could support ignition. If tails and behavior match vapour-region phenomena (e.g., contemporaneous vapor activity), treat as atmospheric rather than solid celestial body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic differences between images formed by droplets, prisms/crystals, and specula
rubrics_metrics.description: Images produced by water droplets (irides), prisms/crystals, and reflecting surfaces differ in color distribution and location; some images are real (in the medium) while others are apparent to the eye because of optical geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare: colors seen through a crystal/prism will differ in place and character from true irides seen in clouds; filling a glass vessel with water under light can produce real colors similar to natural irides. Use controlled experiments with droplets, prisms, and concave/convex surfaces to distinguish the causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concave speculum focusing and ignition criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A concave mirror (speculum) can concentrate solar rays to a focus and ignite material at the focus because many rays are reflected to converge; the concentrating effect depends on the portion of the spherical mirror and its curvature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce ignition: use a concave reflecting surface that collects many nearly-perpendicular rays and brings them to a common point; larger mirror portion and appropriate curvature increase intensity and speed of heating. The concentration effect is weaker for planar mirrors or poorly curved portions; use geometry (centers of circles and arcs) to design focusing surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting strength (vis) of reflected rays
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensity of reflected rays depends on (a) perpendicularity of incidence (perpendicular reflections are strongest), (b) proximity and length of rays (closer rays accumulate greater force), and (c) curvature and size of the reflecting surface (larger and appropriately curved surfaces aggregate more rays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reflected illumination, account for how many rays return near-perpendicularly to a point and how adjacent rays cohere: the nearer and more numerous the contributing rays, the greater the perceived brightness/force. Use this to interpret why some reflections ignite or produce intense images while others are faint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry and cause of twilight (crepusculum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twilight arises because the first solar rays that illuminate the air touch denser vapours near the earth or are impeded by the earth's body, so a region of illumination (crepusculum) begins before sunrise (or persists after sunset) depending on the altitude of vapours and earth-sun geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute onset/duration by geometry: consider the circle of the horizon and lines of rays intersecting vapour layers; vapour altitude determines how many hours before sunrise (or after sunset) twilight appears. Use the same chord/arc/trigonometric procedures as for rainbow measurement to compute the angular times of crepusculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational method for distinguishing real vs imagined solar images (e.g., in deliquium/fainting)
rubrics_metrics.description: When observers see a sunlike image (e.g., during fainting), the image may be produced by reflection in a nearby speculum or by rays in the environment rather than indicating the sun's actual position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by placing a known reflecting surface (speculum under water, concave mirror) or by noting whether the perceived image follows predicted geometric relations; check if the image corresponds to an actual external luminous body or is an optical artifact produced by local reflections.
